references.organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
references.title: Treatment and Intervention for Autism Spectrum Disorder
references.summary: Describes speech and language therapy, occupational therapy, developmental approaches, and behavioral approaches. Supports selecting help around an individual's needs, not a single treatment for everyone.

references.title: Augmentative and Alternative Communication (AAC)
references.summary: Explains gestures, pictures, communication boards, and speech-generating devices. AAC has no prerequisite milestones and can support language alongside speech. A speech-language pathologist can assess and customize access.

references.organization: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence
references.title: CG170: Autism spectrum disorder in under 19s — support and management
references.summary: Section 1.3.1 recommends developmentally appropriate, professionally delivered play-based social-communication support with caregiver involvement. Sections 1.4.1–1.4.9 emphasize communication needs, physical health, the environment, functional assessment, and quality-of-life goals when addressing distressing or unsafe behavior.

references.title: Caregiver skills training for families of children with developmental delays or disabilities: introduction (2022)
references.summary: Describes a structured caregiver training package for families of children aged 2–9 years. It aims to support engagement, communication, positive behavior, and daily-living skills through everyday activities with trained facilitators.

references.title: Hyman, Levy & Myers (2020): Identification, Evaluation, and Management of Children With Autism Spectrum Disorder
references.summary: A clinical report on individualized support, co-occurring conditions, communication, and interventions. It discusses evidence limitations and the need to connect services to functional goals and review outcomes.

lessons.title: Speech, language & AAC
lessons.summary: Support understanding and expression using speech, gestures, pictures, or a communication device.
benefits: More ways to express wants, needs, choices, and refusal.
Support for understanding language and everyday conversations.
Communication access even when speaking is difficult.
lessons.limitations: AAC and speech-language therapy are individualized. AAC is not a guarantee of spoken language, and speech is not the only meaningful outcome.
lessons.professional: A speech-language pathologist can assess communication and help choose an accessible system.

segments.heading: Every way of communicating counts
segments.caption: Speech, gestures, pictures, and devices can all help a child share a message.

segments.heading: More than spoken words
segments.caption: Speech-language therapy can support understanding, expression, and communication with other people.

segments.heading: A picture can carry a message
segments.caption: AAC offers another route to express a choice, a need, or a refusal.

segments.heading: Access comes before performance
segments.caption: There are no prerequisite milestones for AAC. It can be used alongside speech.

segments.heading: Make it fit the child
segments.caption: An SLP can adapt vocabulary and access. Meaningful communication matters more than saying words on demand.

segments.heading: Learn with a qualified professional
segments.caption: Benefits differ by child. Original educational animation, not treatment instructions. References: ASHA; CDC.

lessons.title: Occupational therapy
lessons.summary: Help a child participate in daily routines, play, and self-care in ways that suit their abilities.
benefits: Support for dressing, eating, and other daily routines.
Adaptations for motor, sensory, and environmental barriers.
Practical goals that matter at home and school.
lessons.limitations: Evidence differs across occupational therapy techniques. Sensory activities do not help every child; a sensory-based intervention should have clear goals and its effect should be reviewed.
lessons.professional: An occupational therapist assesses participation and designs an individualized plan with the child and family.

segments.heading: Make everyday life more accessible
segments.caption: Occupational therapy focuses on participating in daily activities, not changing who a child is.

segments.heading: Choose a meaningful goal
segments.caption: Goals may involve dressing, eating, play, or taking part in a classroom routine.

segments.heading: Change the task or environment
segments.caption: An OT may adapt tools, break down a task, or reduce a sensory barrier.

segments.heading: Comfort supports participation
segments.caption: Motor and sensory needs differ. A useful adaptation for one child may not suit another.

segments.heading: Check whether it helps
segments.caption: Evidence varies by technique. Agree on a functional goal and review progress with the therapist.

segments.heading: Support, not a cure
segments.caption: An OT individualizes the plan. Original educational animation, not an exercise prescription. References: CDC; AAP.

lessons.title: Play-based developmental support
lessons.summary: Use enjoyable, developmentally appropriate play to support shared engagement and communication.
benefits: Opportunities for reciprocal communication and shared enjoyment.
Learning within interests and everyday play.
Caregivers can participate with professional coaching.
lessons.limitations: Play-based approaches differ and outcomes vary. No single branded program is best for every child. This guide does not teach a specific therapy protocol.
lessons.professional: A trained professional can choose appropriate play-based social-communication strategies with the family.

segments.heading: Connection through shared enjoyment
segments.caption: Play-based approaches use activities a child finds interesting to support engagement and learning.

segments.heading: Communication can happen in play
segments.caption: Shared attention, turn-taking, and reciprocal communication can be goals of professional support.

segments.heading: Fit the developmental level
segments.caption: NICE recommends adapting social-communication strategies to the child's abilities and needs.

segments.heading: Caregivers can be partners
segments.caption: A trained professional may coach parents or carers to support interaction in everyday activities.

segments.heading: Respect the child's comfort
segments.caption: Shared engagement is not forced eye contact. Enjoyment and willingness to participate matter.

segments.heading: Choose support together
segments.caption: Outcomes vary across approaches. Original educational animation, not a therapy protocol. References: NICE CG170; CDC.

lessons.title: Caregiver skills coaching
lessons.summary: Help caregivers use everyday routines to support engagement, communication, and daily-living skills.
benefits: Consistent communication opportunities during familiar routines.
Practical coaching connected to family priorities.
Support for engagement, daily-living skills, and positive interactions.
lessons.limitations: Caregiver coaching does not replace professional care. The WHO package targets ages 2–9 with developmental delays or disabilities; suitability and local delivery should be discussed with trained services.
lessons.professional: A trained facilitator or appropriate clinician can coach the family, adapt goals, and review progress.

segments.heading: Everyday routines can support learning
segments.caption: Caregiver coaching builds opportunities for communication and engagement into familiar daily activities.

segments.heading: Support the caregiver too
segments.caption: A trained facilitator helps families select practical goals, rather than expecting them to manage alone.

segments.heading: Skills for daily life
segments.caption: WHO caregiver training aims to support communication, engagement, positive behavior, and daily-living skills.

segments.heading: Adapt to the family
segments.caption: Time, resources, language, and the child's needs influence which strategies are workable.

segments.heading: Coaching is not a replacement for care
segments.caption: The WHO package targets children aged 2 to 9. Discuss suitability and support with trained services.

segments.heading: Small goals, shared review
segments.caption: Progress differs between families. Original educational animation, not the WHO course. References: WHO CST; NICE CG170.

lessons.title: Positive behavior support & ABA
lessons.summary: Understand distress or unsafe behavior and support useful skills through individualized, respectful care.
benefits: Identify communication, health, or environmental needs behind distress.
Support useful communication and safer alternatives.
Review outcomes that improve daily life rather than compliance alone.
lessons.limitations: ABA and other behavioral approaches vary widely, and they are not interchangeable. Evidence and acceptability differ. An autism diagnosis alone does not determine whether a particular approach is appropriate.
lessons.professional: Use a qualified multidisciplinary team or behavioral professional who works with the child and family, considers assent, and measures meaningful outcomes.

segments.heading: Start by understanding the need
segments.caption: Distress or unsafe behavior may be linked to pain, communication barriers, or an overwhelming environment.

segments.heading: Assessment before a strategy
segments.caption: NICE recommends checking health and environmental causes, then using functional assessment where appropriate.

segments.heading: Build useful alternatives
segments.caption: Behavioral approaches, including ABA, may support communication and daily-living skills. Programs vary widely.

segments.heading: Quality of life is the goal
segments.caption: Choose meaningful goals with professionals and family. Respect the child's comfort, preferences, and willingness.

segments.heading: Not obedience at any cost
segments.caption: Do not punish distress or target harmless differences just to appear typical. Review concerns with qualified professionals.

segments.heading: Individual support, measured outcomes
segments.caption: There is no one-size-fits-all program. Original educational animation, not behavior-management instructions. References: NICE CG170; CDC.
